question: Which tactical patterns keep coming back in the King's Indian, and how do you count your way to the right move before a trap springs?
outcomes: Counts attackers, guards and recaptures before a capture or pawn push in a King's Indian position
Plays the ...b5 gambit idea: removes a guard of e4 by offering a pawn and then captures on e4 once the count favours Black
Knows the knight trade on g3 (...h6, ...g5, ...Nh5) and finds the move that keeps the key pawn guarded
Recognises the queen-and-bishop battery on h6 and avoids the pawn push that runs into it
Retreats the bishop in the f4 chain instead of capturing a pawn that is guarded twice

Plans and the claim that traps work on habit: [H]/[I] labelled in the text

steps.text: **What you will be able to do.** Traps in this opening repeat: a pawn with too few guards, a trade that removes a guard, a capture that opens a line. You will run one three-part check before you move (attackers, guards, recaptures), play the ...b5 gambit and see why it works, see how a knight trade on g3 can win the d4 pawn, and meet the h6 battery and the f4 capture. Every trap here is machine-checked.

**A gambit that is played.** In the line with h3 and Bd3, Black meets cxd5 with the pawn sacrifice ...b5. Of 164 master games here, 73 chose it. White usually takes with the knight (51 games) or the bishop (17) [V]. The sacrifice works only because of one fact about e4. Watch what the capture on b5 does to its guards.

steps.title: Does the knight capture on e4 work?
steps.prompt: Predict each, then check. If you want an example first, step through the gambit board again.

steps.text: **The rule behind it.** Count who takes first and what each capture gives up. A capture pays when you gain more than you give over the whole exchange; equal numbers of attackers and guards do not settle it. The gambit removes a guard (the knight) by offering it a pawn. This is the first of the three counts: **attackers, guards, recaptures**. [H] A pawn sacrifice that deflects a guard pays off best when your pieces already aim at the same square. Name another square where you could try it.

**A trade that loads a guard.** Black pushes ...h6 and ...g5 to drive the bishop back, then the knight jumps to h5 and takes on g3. White recaptures with the h-pawn. The trade works for Black only when it leaves d4 with one guard too few, so ...exd4 wins a pawn. The next count is **recaptures**: who retakes after each capture? Step through the line where White answers correctly.

steps.text: **When the trade works.** The knight trade on g3 wins a pawn only if the pawn on d4 has lost a guard. Count the guards of d4 before the trade, then the recapture. Here the second guard of d4 is the knight on f3, with the queen behind it. [I] Whenever a plan relies on a single guard of a key pawn, a move that removes that guard gives the opponent a free shot.

**Queen behind bishop.** With a bishop on g5 and the queen on d2, both aim at h6, one behind the other: a *battery*. If a black pawn steps to h6, the bishop can take it and the queen stands ready to retake, so the bishop is guarded. Usually ...h6 simply asks the bishop a question; with the battery in place it hands White a pawn. Look at the original position again and count.

steps.title: Does ...h6 ask a question or lose a pawn?
steps.prompt: Predict each, then check. If you want an example first, step through the battery board again.

steps.text: **The battery check.** Before a pawn push next to your king, count the attackers of the square it enters, including pieces that move onto the same line later. A battery is two pieces on one line: count both. With the queen on d1, nothing can retake on h6 after Bxh6 Bxh6, so White has given a bishop for a pawn. With the queen on d2 it can.

**A pawn attacks the bishop.** In the locked chain Black's pawn reaches f4 and attacks the bishop on e3. The bishop can take the pawn, but the pawn is guarded twice. Count first: **attackers, guards**. The sensible retreat is to f2. Of the master games that reached this position, every one played that bishop move [V].

steps.text: **Typical mistakes.** For Black: capturing on e4 before the sacrifice, and pushing a pawn into the battery. For White: castling or Bd2 after the knight lands on e4, Nd2 after the knight jumps to h5, and capturing the pawn on f4. These were chosen because each looks natural; [H] we have not measured how often players make them. Each one is checked by the engine at depth 16. Now unlabelled tests: in some, the trap is absent.

steps.prompt: Teach it back. Imagine a club player who has never met these traps. In your own words write: the idea (the three counts: attackers, guards, recaptures), when it works, one example a beginner can set up on a board, and one warning.

steps.text: **Recap and self-check.** Count attackers and guards before any capture or push, then who recaptures. The ...b5 gambit lures a guard away from e4. The knight trade on g3 wins a pawn only when d4 has lost a guard. The battery on h6 makes a pawn push cost material. The pawn on f4 is guarded twice, so retreat. Self-check: did your teach-back say when the count helps, when it fails, and give one real position? If not, write that line again.
